rationale: A wins because it keeps the story on the supplied facts and turns missing facts into gates, not decorations. Its line, "No link between resale and the dividend was supplied," is the adult supervision this assignment needed; B walks straight past that guardrail with "a public retailer answering to shareholders has a hard time cheering on resale, which cannibalizes new-product margin." B has useful reporter shapes, especially the nondisclosure angle, but too many of its best hooks require facts REI did not give us.
gaps_in_A: "Your old tent now has a trade-in price at the local REI" is too cute for the fact base; the update says used gear can be traded for credit, not that tents are accepted or priced in-store.

"resale and repair stop being a side channel and become something every store has to staff and stock" leans beyond the facts; staffing, stocking, and on-site repair capacity are exactly the proof still needed.
A treats the undisclosed used-gear sales share as an uncomfortable question but mostly refuses the accountability angle; the missing denominator could itself be a sharper story.
gaps_in_B: "pushing customers to buy used" is not in the update; trade-in and repair expansion does not prove a buy-used push.
"a public retailer answering to shareholders has a hard time cheering on resale, which cannibalizes new-product margin" is a smart-sounding thesis built on unsupported competitor economics.
"REI won't say how much of its business is used gear" overstates "not disclosed" as an active refusal; that difference matters if you are not trying to hand a reporter a correction.
"Trade-in counters and repair benches arrive" invents store infrastructure; all we know is members can get repairs at any store, not whether benches or technicians are on-site.
